title: The Scribe Who Invented Quarantine Law
event_summary: The Rector and Great Council of Ragusa, guided by the city's notary and legal scribe Jacob of Padua, passed the 'Trentina' — a statute requiring all arriving ships and trade caravans from plague-affected regions to isolate on the nearby island of Mrkan or in the town of Cavtat for thirty days before entering the city. This was the first codified, legally enforced isolation period in recorded history, predating Venice's more famous 'quarantina' of 1423 by nearly half a century. Jacob drafted the precise legal framework that made violation a criminal offense punishable by fine and exile, transforming an ad hoc practice into reproducible statutory law.
why_forgotten: Venice's later forty-day quarantine system became the etymological and historical standard, overshadowing Ragusa's earlier innovation. Ragusa was a small city-state whose archives were largely inaccessible to Western scholars for centuries, especially after its absorption into the Habsburg Empire and later Yugoslavia. Venetian historiographical dominance meant that Mediterranean public health innovation was credited almost exclusively to Venice and Italian city-states.
why_it_matters: Every modern quarantine law, from COVID-19 lockdown orders to WHO International Health Regulations, descends from the principle that a government can legally compel isolation of healthy individuals based on disease exposure — a concept first codified in Ragusa's 1377 statute. The idea that public health authority could override individual liberty and commercial freedom through written law, rather than royal decree or religious edict, established the legal DNA of modern epidemiological governance. Ragusa proved that a small polity could survive a pandemic not through military power but through bureaucratic innovation.
